query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In an initially single‐phase high-entropy alloy, plastic deformation at intermediate temperatures drives dislocation‐assisted diffusion of the principal elements to grain boundaries, where the enhanced diffusion—overcoming the alloy’s inherently sluggish kinetics—induces rapid nanosegregation that reduces grain boundary cohesion and triggers brittle intergranular cracking even without the formation of large intermetallic precipitates.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single-phase compositionally complex HEA (for example, an equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi alloy) with uniformly distributed constituents and no preexisting grain-boundary precipitates.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled plastic deformation at intermediate temperatures and moderate strain rates to promote dislocation motion and enhanced elemental diffusion.
generation.conditions: Intermediate service temperatures and moderate strain rates where dislocation activity and atomic mobility are sufficient to drive non-equilibrium, fast grain boundary segregation, yet remain below those that would trigger significant grain coarsening or conventional intermetallic precipitation.
generation.mechanism: During deformation, dislocation motion creates local stress fields and vacancies that enhance the mobility of principal elements. This accelerated diffusion, in spite of the alloy’s normally sluggish kinetic behavior, results in rapid nanosegregation at grain boundaries, weakening their cohesion and promoting intergranular brittle cracking.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undeformed alloy, deformed samples will show measurable increases in the concentration of specific principal elements at grain boundaries (as determined by atom probe tomography or EDS) and a corresponding decrease in toughness, with fracture surfaces displaying more intergranular features. The degree of embrittlement should correlate with the severity of the imposed deformation conditions.
generation.baseline: The as-synthesized, undeformed HEA exhibiting homogeneous chemistry and good toughness with predominantly transgranular ductile fracture under mechanical loading.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate under intermediate temperature and moderate strain-rate conditions. At lower temperatures, limited diffusion may prevent significant segregation, while at higher temperatures other mechanisms (such as grain-boundary sliding or conventional precipitation) might control the deformation behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature and strain rate threshold for the onset of fast nanosegregation and embrittlement is not fully quantified and may vary with the specific alloy chemistry and processing history.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identically processed single-phase HEA specimens. Subject one set to controlled plastic deformation at an intermediate temperature (e.g., 600°C) with a moderate strain rate, while maintaining the other set as an undeformed control. After deformation, characterize both sets using high-resolution chemical analysis (e.g., atom probe tomography or energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy) to quantify the elemental distribution at grain boundaries. Perform mechanical testing (e.g., fracture toughness and tensile tests) and fractography to assess the failure mode.
measurements: Grain boundary elemental composition (concentration profiles of Cr, Ni, Mn)
Fractographic analysis to determine intergranular vs transgranular cracking
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the deformed specimens do not show a significant enrichment of principal elements at grain boundaries compared to the control, or if the toughness remains comparable (with no increase in intergranular fracture features) despite the imposed deformation, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are novel high-temperature structural materials based on the design concept of high-entropy alloys (HEA) [, , ]. The multi-principal element characteristic of RHEAs leads to unique microstructures and remarkable properties, such as extremely high melting points, excellent high-temperature strengths, outstanding thermal stabilities, and exceptional creep, corrosion, and oxidation resistances [, , , ]. Owing to these advantages, RHEAs not only exhibit a significant application potential in aerospace and nuclear energy industries as high-temperature load-bearing or thermal protection structures, but also are regarded as an important development direction of high-temperature structural materials. Considering the crucial influence of microstructures on the properties, microstructure control is a meaningful approach to optimize and improve the macroscopic properties of alloys [,]. The element grain boundary segregation structure proposed in recent years provides extraordinary advantages to enhance the properties of alloys [,]. cited_evidence.text: Segregation of minor alloying elements to GBs often embrittles conventional alloys (, ). Grain refinement is an effective way to evade GB embrittlement because more interfaces reduce the level of individual GB segregation (). In contrast, multiple principal constitutive elements in HEAs can segregate into GBs instead of trace alloying elements. In HEAs, grain refinement can assist the segregation of principal constitutive elements to GBs and even lead to the formation of brittle intermetallic phases at GBs (). For example, Cr-rich bcc phases and L10-NiMn phases precipitate at GBs in nanocrystalline Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA (grain size, ~50 nm) after annealing at 450°C for only 5 min, which reduces the ductility substantially (). In addition, previous studies show that Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEAs with the grain sizes from 4.4 to 155 μm all exhibit loss of ductility at intermediate temperatures, irrespective of grain size in this range (Fig. 1). Microalloying with B in Fe-Mn steels has been reported to delay temper embrittlement at 450°C (). cited_evidence.text: To evade the fast segregation of principal elements Ni, Cr, and Mn into GBs, we propose to migrate the fast segregation of these elements from GBs to the preexisting precipitates that are enriched with principal embrittling elements, especially for alloys used at intermediate and high temperatures, because intermetallic compounds can deform at high temperatures, although they reduce the ductility of the alloys at room temperature compared with the single-phase alloys. On the basis of the chemical compositions of four possible GB precipitates in the Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA reported by previous studies (see table S1) (, , ), the Cr-rich σ phase absorbs Cr elements, while it repels other element segregation to GBs. Otto et al. found that GBs are rich in Ni and have no obvious segregation of embrittling elements Mn and Cr when Cr-rich σ phases were precipitated at GBs (, ). In addition, without Mn, Ni segregated in σ phase–free GBs is beneficial to GB cohesion.
